data.claude_summary: When the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) took effect, did it actually boost trade? Among French multiproduct firms, CETA prompted a reallocation toward core, highest-volume products—consistent with intensified competition from other EU producers entering the Canadian market simultaneously. The methodological contribution is significant: matrix completion requires weaker assumptions than standard gravity-model estimators and handles multidimensional counterfactuals that conventional approaches cannot.
data.key_takeaway: Causal machine learning reveals that trade agreements create simultaneous winners and losers at the product level that aggregate statistics conceal—a warning against relying on average treatment effects for policy design.

data.claude_summary: When eight frontier LLMs are assigned geopolitical roles in a simulated Greenland sovereignty crisis — spanning the U.S., Denmark, NATO, Russia, Canada, and Greenland itself — their behavior reveals systematic differences in how AI models handle coercion and alliance norms. Across 3,604 completed games, all eight models became significantly more escalatory under coercive framing (four-action escalation rising from 10.7% to 28.6%). Chinese-origin models weighted power differently from Western-origin models when playing the U.S. role, and peaceful acquisition emerged in only 1.9% of clean games. The paper uses inverse game theory to recover each model's structural utility parameters, positioning the exercise as a behavioral benchmark for LLMs in high-stakes strategic settings.
data.key_takeaway: All tested LLMs escalate significantly under coercive framing, and the structural preferences they encode vary meaningfully by model origin — a practical warning for any organization using frontier AI in strategic or policy analysis.

data.centre_angle: This survey argues that agentic AI systems proposed for social good are systematically under-specified: they invoke universal goals while omitting the geographic and institutional context that determines whether those goals can be meaningfully pursued. From CAMO's perspective on AI Algorithms & Data, the finding points to a structural design problem — when systems are trained and evaluated without grounding in local legal, political, or cultural conditions, accountability becomes unenforceable by design. The paper's call for minimal reporting standards resonates with CAMO's broader interest in the conditions under which algorithmic decisions can be trusted and audited; as CAMO's work on dynamic selection and reinforcement bias shows, ignoring the context in which data is generated and decisions are made produces systematic distortions that are invisible until deployment.
data.claude_summary: A structured survey of 112 papers on agentic AI for social good finds a troubling pattern: the systems most likely to affect vulnerable communities are least likely to be grounded in any specific geographic, legal, or cultural context. Seventy-three percent of papers specify no geographic setting at all. The gap is sharpest in institutional domains — papers addressing peace, justice, and governance (SDG 16) specify geography only 13% of the time, compared with 37–40% for health and ecological papers. Only 25% of papers report any real-world deployment. The authors argue this constitutes 'moral abstraction': treating institutional good as universally portable in ways that health interventions are not. They propose a minimal reporting standard for context-specific, participatory, and accountable agentic AI.
data.key_takeaway: AI systems designed for social good that omit geographic and institutional context cannot be held accountable to the communities they claim to serve — and the evidence suggests most currently do.

data.centre_angle: This study argues that sustained AI use in academic settings produces a compounding fatigue that erodes motivation and attentional capacity — not merely technical friction, but a structural disincentive to effortful engagement. CAMO's own experimental work with professional illustrators — published as 'Better Technology, Worse Motivation' — found that AI assistance reduced the returns to effort and prompted a strategic retreat to lower-quality outputs; the AI fatigue construct offers a complementary mechanism through which that demotivation may accumulate in repeated-use settings.
data.claude_summary: What happens when students use AI tools so extensively that the tools themselves become a source of exhaustion? This grounded-theory study of 1,054 university students across three Philippine universities identifies five distinct dimensions of AI fatigue: Cognitive Overload, Motivational Disengagement, Moral Unease, Physical Strain, and Attentional Drift. Crucially, the researchers argue these pressures do not operate independently but accumulate and reinforce one another in a stage-based progression. The study positions AI fatigue as a construct separate from technostress or digital fatigue — one specific to sustained, mediated interaction with AI in goal-oriented tasks. The conceptual model is exploratory and based on self-reported open-ended responses; instrument validation and scale development are flagged as necessary next steps.
data.key_takeaway: Repeated AI use may not just save effort — it may erode the motivation and attention needed for high-quality work, a dynamic that managers deploying AI tools at scale should not assume will self-correct.

data.centre_angle: This paper addresses a genuine gap in decision-support methodology: optimisation models find efficient solutions but not necessarily stakeholder-relevant ones, while participatory methods consult stakeholders but explore too narrow a solution space. data.claude_summary: Complex planning decisions—such as how to decarbonise a university campus energy system—typically force a choice between rigorous optimisation models and structured stakeholder consultation. This paper proposes a method called Value-Focused Modelling to Generate Alternatives (VF-MGA) that runs both in tandem: stakeholder objectives shape which alternatives an optimisation algorithm generates, and those alternatives are then scored against stakeholder preferences through multi-criteria analysis. Applied to a real campus case with eleven stakeholder groups, the method produced 691 near-optimal configurations, surfaced options that pure optimisation would have ignored, and revealed where stakeholder preferences genuinely converge or conflict. The framework is presented as generalisable beyond energy systems to any complex planning domain.
data.key_takeaway: Combining stakeholder objective-setting with large-scale optimisation generates planning alternatives that are both technically near-optimal and genuinely relevant to the people affected by the decision.

data.centre_angle: This audit finds that generative search engines are routinely citing AI-generated web sources — at a rate of roughly one in six citations — without distinguishing them from authoritative human-produced content. From CAMO's perspective on the statistical and governance foundations of trustworthy AI-driven decisions, this is a data-quality problem with systemic consequences: if the retrieval layer of AI systems cannot reliably filter synthetic content, downstream inferences and recommendations built on those outputs inherit an invisible layer of circularity. Organisations deploying AI for research, compliance, or market intelligence need to treat citation provenance as an auditable input, not an assumed given.
data.claude_summary: An audit of four generative search engines — ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity — finds that roughly 16% of sources cited in responses to real-world queries show evidence of being AI-generated, across health, politics, and environmental topics. The study used 712 human-generated queries and identified specific web domains that repeatedly surface as synthetic sources. The engines also exhibit a narrow citation pattern: a small set of domains is cited frequently, while a large tail of domains appears only once or twice. The finding raises a structural reliability problem: when AI-generated content is treated as equivalent to authoritative sources inside the response loop, errors can compound without users being aware of the origin or quality of the underlying information.
data.key_takeaway: About one in six sources cited by leading generative search engines shows evidence of being AI-generated, meaning decisions informed by these tools may be grounded in content with no independent authoritative basis.

data.centre_angle: This paper argues that AI disclosure in research has stalled at the level of output attribution—documenting what AI wrote or generated—while the more consequential question of cognitive agency remains unaddressed. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the implication is organizational as much as scholarly: the same ambiguity that undermines academic accountability also surfaces inside firms deploying AI in knowledge work, where it is rarely clear whether a decision was originated by a human or proposed by a system. CAMO's work on the hidden competence penalties employees face when AI use is visible (see 'Research: The Hidden Penalty of Using AI at Work') suggests that without credible process-level disclosure, organizations will continue to conflate AI-assisted output with unassisted capability—with real consequences for evaluation, trust, and incentive design.
data.claude_summary: Scientific publishing has no standard way to document how AI was used during research—only what it produced. This paper identifies that gap as substantive, not cosmetic: current disclosure norms cannot distinguish a researcher who independently conceived a study from one who adopted an AI-suggested direction, or one who critically evaluated AI outputs from one who accepted them uncritically. The proposed PAIRED framework reorients disclosure around decision points in the research process, generates both an author log and a publisher-facing summary from the same inputs, and embeds logging triggers into the workflow to prevent selective omission. The authors demonstrate the framework through worked examples and propose embedding it directly into AI research platforms.
data.key_takeaway: Without process-level records of how AI was used—not just what it produced—neither research institutions nor organizations can reliably assess the intellectual contribution behind AI-assisted work.

data.centre_angle: This paper argues that the binary choice between banning and permitting GenAI in assessment is a false dilemma, and that governance should instead follow the logic of what a valid inference requires. From CAMO's perspective on AI & Jobs, the deeper implication is organizational: as workplaces increasingly embed GenAI in professional workflows, educational institutions face the same challenge firms do — how to design evaluation systems that remain meaningful when AI assistance is ubiquitous. CAMO's research on the hidden competence penalties associated with AI use at work ('Research: The Hidden Penalty of Using AI at Work') suggests that how AI use is signaled and interpreted matters enormously; a generation trained under inconsistent AI-governance norms will enter firms where those ambiguities have real career consequences.
data.claude_summary: How should institutions govern generative AI in STEM assessments — ban it, permit it, or require it? This paper proposes a framework rooted in Evidence-Centered Design that treats GenAI as a built-in design variable rather than an external threat. The core argument: the right governance stance depends on what skill is being measured. Restrict GenAI when it would short-circuit the inference between student output and target ability. Allow bounded use when it handles peripheral demands without revealing the core skill. Require it when the target competency is disciplinary AI interaction itself — prompting, critiquing, revising — and when process artifacts can be captured and scored. The framework is demonstrated in an introductory physics course, where AI-interaction competencies proved observable and scorable.
data.key_takeaway: Governing GenAI in assessment is not about prohibition or permission but about specifying precisely which competency is being measured and designing tasks where human reasoning remains visible regardless of AI involvement.

data.claude_summary: Using 5 million job postings from Beijing (2018–2024), this study builds a neighborhood-level index of GenAI exposure and finds that the technology's impact is spatially uneven and paradoxical. Districts with the highest GenAI exposure have seen wage growth stall since 2023, even as they continue drawing highly skilled workers — a dynamic the authors call a 'high-skill trap.' The mechanism is task de-skilling and labor-market crowding: GenAI erodes the cognitive premium that once justified high wages in knowledge-intensive roles. The findings challenge standard skill-biased technological change theory and suggest that GenAI may deepen rather than bridge intra-urban economic divides.

data.centre_angle: This paper argues that AI safety governance has a blind spot: nearly all attention goes to preventing loss of control, while the operational question of what to do when prevention fails remains underdeveloped. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic decision-making and trustworthy AI, the implication is that organizations deploying consequential AI systems face not just a technical design problem but an institutional one — who holds authority to trigger a circuit-breaker, how are adversarial incidents distinguished from accidental ones, and what governance structures make proportional escalation credible? These are organizational questions as much as engineering ones, and they sit upstream of any specific deployment decision.
data.claude_summary: What happens when an AI system can no longer be controlled — not just in theory, but as an operational emergency? This paper argues that current AI safety discourse is too narrowly focused on prevention, leaving a gap in response planning. It proposes a taxonomy distinguishing scenarios where regaining control is extremely costly (and therefore manageable through containment and threat neutralization) from those where control is effectively impossible (requiring resilience investments that limit AI's attack surface in advance). It further separates accidental from adversarial loss-of-control events, mapping three severity classes to specific incident-response protocols. The framework is explicitly modeled on emergency management disciplines, treating catastrophic AI loss of control as an incident type requiring structured, proportional governance — not just better alignment research.
data.key_takeaway: Organizations need incident-response frameworks for AI loss of control — not just alignment safeguards — because prevention alone is insufficient governance.
